pronunciation.approximation: 'RAH-tah-toskr' — stress on the first syllable, as in every Old Norse word; all vowels short; the final -r is the nominative ending, lightly sounded as in modern Icelandic Ratatoskur.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Ratatoskr is a compound whose second element is toskr, 'tusk, tooth'. The first is usually taken as rati, 'borer, auger' — the very name of the gimlet Óðinn drives through the mountain in the mead-myth — whence the standard gloss 'drill-tooth'. A rival reading takes rata, 'to travel, find one's way', yielding 'travel-tooth', a fit almost too neat for the squirrel who runs the world-tree's trunk; Cleasby-Vigfusson prints the word, Lindow registers both derivations, and the dispute is honest. Ratatoskr is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: normalized Old Norse writes the name in plain Latin letters, so the ASCII form loses nothing — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter to restore.

domains.title: Squirrel of Yggdrasil
domains.subtitle: The Drill-Tooth, the Malicious Messages, and the Trunk of the World-Ash
domains.lead: Ratatoskr is the squirrel of the world-ash Yggdrasill: the small tireless runner of Grímnismál who bears the eagle's words down from the crown and carries Níðhǫggr's answers back up from the roots — and whom Snorri names as the courier of öfundarorð, malicious messages, between the two great enemies of the tree.

cards.name: Yggdrasill's Ash
cards.desc: The world-tree itself, 'the greatest and best of all trees': Ratatoskr's whole road, from the eagle's crown to the roots over Hvergelmir.

cards.name: The Unnamed Eagle
cards.desc: The great eagle perched in the ash's limbs, wise in many things — with the hawk Veðrfölnir sitting between its eyes.

cards.name: Níðhǫggr
cards.desc: The Malice-Striker: the serpent at the root in Niflheimr who gnaws the ash and sucks the corpses of the dead — the eagle's eternal correspondent.

cards.name: Veðrfölnir
cards.desc: The hawk between the eagle's eyes — the watcher in the crown, witness to every word the squirrel carries down.

symbols.name: The world-ash
symbols.meaning: The vertical axis of the cosmos — and the only road Ratatoskr ever runs, crown to root and back

symbols.name: The malicious message (öfundarorð)
symbols.meaning: Snorri's word for the squirrel's cargo: slander carried between powers too proud to speak to each other

symbols.name: The drill-tooth
symbols.meaning: The name itself — rati, the boring auger, and toskr, the tusk: a tooth that drills, a tongue that bores

symbols.name: The hawk between the eyes
symbols.meaning: Veðrfölnir, set in the eagle's brow — the unblinking audit above the squirrel's errands

mythology.lead: Ratatoskr's dossier is two passages long and perfectly cut: one stanza of Grímnismál and one chapter of Gylfaginning. Between them they give him a road, a cargo, and a character — and nothing else in the corpus adds a word.

myths.title: The Squirrel's Stanza
myths.text: In Grímnismál, Óðinn — masked and bound between the fires of King Geirrøðr — recites the inhabitants of the world-ash, and the squirrel gets his stanza: Ratatoskr is the íkorni who must run on Yggdrasill's ash; the eagle's words he must carry from above and tell to Níðhǫggr below. The verb is skal — 'shall, must': the running is not a habit but an office, written into the tree's economy as fixedly as the dew that falls from its branches. In a single stanza the Edda gives the smallest creature in the cosmos a route that spans it.

myths.title: The Suffering Ash
myths.text: The stanzas around the squirrel build the tree's full menagerie: four harts — Dáinn and Dvalinn, Duneyrr and Duraþrór — bite the new shoots; more serpents lie beneath the ash than any unwise ape would think, Góinn and Móinn, Grábakr and Grafvölluðr, Ófnir and Sváfnir, and they gnaw the roots forever; and the poem closes the survey with its most famous sentence: the ash of Yggdrasill suffers agony, more than men know — the hart bites from above, the trunk rots at the side, and Níðhǫggr gnaws from below. Ratatoskr runs his messages through a tree that is being eaten alive at every level.

myths.title: Malice Up and Down the Trunk
myths.text: Snorri's prose fills out the stanza into a portrait. An eagle sits in the limbs of the ash, and it has knowledge of many things, and between its eyes sits a hawk called Veðrfölnir. A squirrel called Ratatoskr springs up and down the ash and bears öfundarorð — words of malice, slander-tidings — between the eagle and Níðhǫggr. Where Grímnismál described a messenger, Snorri describes an agent provocateur: the squirrel does not merely deliver the correspondence of the crown and the root, he keeps the feud alive, carrying each insult to the ear best placed to feel it. The four harts and the wells of Urðr and Mímir complete the chapter — but the squirrel is its only animal with an errand.

myths.title: The Dragon at the Root
myths.text: The lower terminus of Ratatoskr's road is the worst address in the cosmos. Snorri sets the third root of the ash over Niflheimr and the spring Hvergelmir, and there Níðhǫggr gnaws the root from below while countless serpents coil with him. Völuspá gives the Malice-Striker his other aspect: in Nástrǫnd, the corpse-shore, he sucks the bodies of the dead, and the wolf tears men — and at the poem's end the dark dragon comes flying up from Niðafjǫll, bearing corpses on his wings, in the last light before the world sinks. Every word Ratatoskr carries down lands in that ear; every word he carries up rises from it. The squirrel's whole mythology is the maintenance of that terrible conversation.

lore.syncretism: Ratatoskr belongs to a pattern far older and wider than Iceland: the tree that holds the worlds, the eagle in its crown, the serpent at its root. The famous ancient parallel is the Mesopotamian Etana myth, where the eagle and the serpent dwell in the same great tree and their broken pact drives the story — a resemblance scholars have noted for over a century without being able to trace a line of borrowing; Lindow and Simek treat the configuration as a widely distributed world-tree motif rather than a loan. Within the North, the squirrel has no counterpart at all: he is the Edda's own invention, the one member of the tree's menagerie defined by speech rather than appetite. His nearest functional kin are Óðinn's ravens, who likewise range the world and return with words — but the ravens gather news, and Ratatoskr manufactures a feud. Comparativists have also pointed to the squirrel as the classic trickster go-between: small, deniable, and indispensable to enemies who must not be seen to speak.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ratatoskr's afterlife grew with the tree he runs. Padraic Colum's The Children of Odin (1920) carried the squirrel into English-language retellings for children, and every popular handbook since has kept him running. Modern readings have made him the patron of the poisonous go-between — the forwarder of insults, the courier of feuds — a role that has only sharpened in the age of the message-board and the screenshot. He has become a minor star of games and pop culture: a playable god in Smite (2015), and the scene-stealing squirrel of God of War Ragnarök (2022), where the ancient slander-courier is played, faithfully to Snorri, as the most insulting creature in the Nine Realms. In Iceland the name lives on as Ratatoskur, and modern Heathen and Ásatrú retellings keep him as the comic-dark emblem of how small tongues keep great hatreds fed.
lore.extendedMeditation: Ratatoskr is the Edda's smallest cosmological fact and one of its sharpest. The universe is held in a tree; the tree is being eaten from crown to root; and through the middle of the disaster runs a squirrel, up and down, carrying the worst things the top and the bottom can think of to say to each other. Snorri's word for the cargo is exact: öfundarorð — not news, not warnings, but malice. The myth knows something the etiquette books miss, that feuds do not survive on hatred alone but on delivery — that between every great enmity runs some small, quick, indispensable creature who keeps the words fresh. Ratatoskr never appears in a saga, never wins a fight, never speaks a line the sources record. He only carries. And the Edda gives him eternity for it: while the ash stands, the squirrel runs, and the eagle and the dragon never lack for ammunition.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Ratatoskr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚱᛅᛏᛅᛏᚢᛋᚴᛦ (r-a-t-a-t-u-s-k-R, the ᚢ rune writing o and ᛦ the final nominative -r), though no runic attestation survives and the manuscript spelling remains the primary witness. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: ratatoskr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Ratatoskr is an entirely textual creature: no picture stone, runestone, amulet, or toponym preserves him, and the squirrel is otherwise invisible in Norse material culture. His two attestations hang on the great codices: Grímnismál in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), and Gylfaginning in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda and its sister manuscripts (early 14th c.), with the poem's stanza also copied into the Codex Wormianus and the Uppsala Edda tradition. The world-ash itself has material echoes — the tree-and-beasts carvings sometimes compared to Yggdrasill's menagerie — but none can be tied to the squirrel by name. His evidence is the manuscript page alone, which is fitting: Ratatoskr was always made of words.
